title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days, once you have worked through the topics and taken your mocks. The aim now is to sharpen how you read AI audit questions, not to learn new material. Most days take about an hour; the two mock days take longer.
how_it_works: Short reviews spread over several days hold up better than one long session the night before.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan, not a break from it.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with today's plan. Doubling up turns review into cramming.
Practice scores are not scaled exam scores. Use them to find gaps, not to predict a result.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the time of day your exam starts, to test your pace and stamina.

tasks.text: Before you start, decide that whatever the score, you follow tomorrow's plan. The score shows where to look, not how the exam will go.
Take a full timed mock in one sitting at your exam's start time, with your phone away and no notes.
Practice the pace: aim for about 90 seconds a question. Past 2 minutes on one question, choose your best answer, flag it and move on.
If you plan to use your break, take it at the same point today, without pausing the mock, so the clock keeps running.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: One mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. A practice score is not a scaled score, and it can swing from day to day.

days.title: Learn from every miss
days.goal: Trace each mock miss back to the thinking slip behind it, starting with Domain 2. Stop after about 90 minutes, even if some are left.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from yesterday's mock, starting with Domain 2, then Domain 1.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed FIRST or BEST”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list three Domain 2 and three Domain 1 points. Then open the lists and check.
Before you open the principles on which fix works, say why retraining a model is a change that needs testing and approval, not a cure. Then check.

days.remember: A miss you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

days.title: Your biggest gap
days.goal: Work on the domain where your readiness is furthest behind its weight on the exam.

tasks.text: Before opening your focus domain's list, write down what you remember. Then check for gaps.
Answer a short set in that domain, rating how sure you are before you check each answer.
Review first the answers you felt sure of but got wrong. Those are the ones to fix.
For a topic you missed more than once, read its note, then close it and explain the idea in two sentences.
Read the principles on your role: who owns the AI decision, and what the IS auditor does and never does.

days.remember: Weight matters: Domain 2 alone is close to half the exam.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your exam pace sharp with one timed mini mock, and refresh how you audit AI and use AI in the audit.

tasks.text: Take a timed mini mock in one sitting. Watch the pace checks more than the score.
From memory, list three Domain 3 points. Then open the list and check.
Without looking, say why an AI tool's output is a lead and not evidence, then check the note.
Read the principles on how you know the AI does what is claimed.
Read the principles on what matters most: ownership first, then risk ranked by harm.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Read like the exam
days.goal: Sharpen how you read each question and find the AI-specific fact, then work on your second gap.

tasks.text: Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Read the principles on reading the question.
Practice a short set in your second-weakest domain. Before the options, name the priority word and the AI-specific fact.
Redo up to 20 mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.

days.remember: Several options are often true. The priority word and the AI-specific fact decide which one wins.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Recall everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details, so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each domain, recall two points before you open its list. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Say what comes first when an AI system causes harm, then open the principles to check.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your booking, ID and route. Testing online? Run the compatibility check again on the computer you will use, and try PSI's tutorial test (about 30 minutes).

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: answer up to 10 mistake journal questions, then stop. A miss today is a reminder, not a warning.
Read the reminder for the slip you make most often.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your booking is confirmed, and you have checked the ID and exam-day rules in ISACA's AAIA Exam Candidate Guide.
Online: the compatibility check is done and your desk is clear. Test center: your route and travel time are planned.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your pace plan: aim for about 90 seconds a question, near question 40 at 1 hour and question 80 at 2 hours.
Arrive at least 30 minutes early at a test center. Online, you can start check-in up to 30 minutes before your appointment, so log in then.
Recall your break plan, made before today: whether you take it, and at about which question. The clock keeps running during it.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, flag the question and come back to it.

points.text: Who decides: the board approves AI risk appetite, senior management sets tolerances within it and model owners set use-level criteria. The IS auditor assesses and advises, never votes, approves or accepts the risk.
Every model and AI decision needs a named business owner. “The model decided” or “the vendor is accountable” is never the answer; accountability cannot be outsourced.
Inventory first: governance covers only the AI it can see, including AI inside purchased products and AI staff use without approval. Test completeness against independent evidence, not surveys.

AI risk is wider than security: risk assessments weigh likelihood and impact, including harm to the people affected, and are redone when anything material changes. The risk owner chooses the response; the IS auditor assesses the process.
Buying AI moves the work, not the accountability. Expect due diligence, contract rights over model changes and data use, and the organization's own testing; vendor reports are inputs, not assurance.
No owner, no lineage, no reliance: training data needs an owner, traceable origin and the right to use it for this purpose. Deleting source records does not remove what a model memorized.
A trustworthy-AI principle needs a measure, a threshold and an owner before it can be audited. A framework or a management-system certificate does not prove a given model is fair or accurate.
Data before model: show origin and rights to use before quality tests, and judge representativeness against the people the model decides about. A score is only as good as truly unseen test data.

Retraining, new data, prompts, thresholds and vendor model updates are all changes: each needs an impact assessment, testing on the organization's own use, the owner's approval and a rollback. A version is the model plus its code, data and settings.

Oversight must work, not just exist: a person who understands the output, has time to judge and can override or stop it. Near-total agreement in seconds signals automation bias. Affected people need an appeal route.
Monitor decisions, not just servers. Drift shows in production data and outcomes, not on the launch test set, and scheduled retraining does not replace monitoring.

Set acceptance criteria before testing, and check errors by group. Builders do not grade their own model: validation is independent of them, and the IS auditor assesses it, never performs or approves it.

Judge an AI agent by what its account can do, not what its prompt says. Least privilege, its own identity and human approval for high-impact actions bound it; a prompt instruction or a network firewall does not.

Harmful or biased output is an incident even when nothing was breached. Disengage or roll back and preserve evidence first. An ordinary incident closes once service is confirmed, and the problem record carries the root cause. Suspected manipulation stays open.
Build the whole AI audit universe first, including AI in purchased software and business-unit tools, then rank it by the likelihood and impact of harm, not novelty or technical complexity.

Using AI in the audit is audit management's decision: it approves uses and data limits, the tool is validated on known outcomes before anyone relies on it, and audit data stays inside approved services.
Treat human oversight as a control to test, and sample AI decisions by group, confidence and override. A larger random sample can still miss a small group.
Reperform a decision with the model version that made it. Items an AI tool did not flag are untested, not clean.
Records systems produce, such as lineage, logs and alert histories, outrank documents builders write, which outrank what people say. Evidence must match the model version and cover the period.
An AI tool's output is a lead until checked against source records. Rerunning it or asking it to check itself proves nothing.

Findings name condition, criteria, cause and the effect on people and the business, and recommend an outcome for a named owner, not the fix. AI may draft; the IS auditor concludes and discloses its use.

principles.intro: The AAIA mindset principles, one line each. Each day, try to recall a few before you read them, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. What must happen before anything else? Usually ownership, inventory or assessing the risk comes before acting; if an AI system is harming people right now, disengaging it comes first.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what does everything else depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the strongest overall: within the IS auditor's role, closing the control gap rather than patching the model, and covering the most.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which would I defend to the audit committee?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as MOST reliable evidence or MOST effective control. Judge the options on that quality only.
The core purpose or main reason, not a side benefit or a nice extra.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For AI risk, the realistic harm with the widest effect on people and the business, not the newest or most technical threat.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest realistic harm, and to whom?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What the facts point to, such as drift after the input data changed, even if another outcome would be worse.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what do these facts point to?

priority_words.meaning: Flip the logic. Three options do the job; find the one that does it worst or not at all.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is being asked: an action, a risk, a purpose or a piece of evidence.

answering_routine.title: Find the priority word
answering_routine.text: Spot FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY, GREATEST, MOST LIKELY or LEAST before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Check your role and the owner
answering_routine.text: You are the IS auditor unless told otherwise. Who owns this AI decision: the model owner, senior management, the AI governance committee or the board? You assess and recommend; you never retrain, approve or accept the risk.

answering_routine.title: Find the AI-specific fact
answering_routine.text: Spot the fact that changes the answer for AI, such as a retrained model, a vendor update, a new use, an untested group or a reviewer who approves without real review.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options with the wrong role, a tool before ownership or policy, a model fix for a control gap, an absolute word or an action outside scope.

answering_routine.title: Decide between the final two
answering_routine.text: Apply the priority word, then prefer the option that comes earlier, covers more, fixes the cause and keeps the IS auditor independent.

pace: 150 minutes for 90 questions is 100 seconds each. Aiming for about 90 seconds leaves about 15 minutes to review flagged questions.
Checkpoints: around question 40 at 1 hour and question 80 at 2 hours.
Past 2 minutes on one question, choose your best answer, flag it and move on. Never leave a question blank.
AI scenarios can run long. Read the last line first, then scan the scenario for the fact that decides.
One break of up to 10 minutes, with the proctor's permission. The clock keeps running, so it uses most of your review time; plan it before the day.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as a fact or a priority word you missed the first time.
